AfriScan · South Africa · Servitudes, reserves and sites

Secure your servitudes from the air, remotely

We map the structures, cleared ground, fresh excavations and tracks inside the servitudes of your power lines, pipelines, bulk-water mains and rail and road reserves, measure each one to the line and show what changed between dated surveys. Satellite first, your own drone imagery where you already fly, and a person reviews every result before it reaches you.

Request a proposal See sample outputs
  • Your servitude widthsMeasured to what is registered, or your standard
  • Every 500 mRated for encroachment density
  • Your drone imageryAnalysed with the same method

Our published sample is from Mozambique: the route of a high-pressure gas pipeline, with its 100 m band, on a Copernicus Sentinel-2 scene of 2 August 2026. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2026.

The rules behind the work Civil Aviation Regulations Part 101 · POPIA · SANRAL Act s48 · NEMA EIA Regulations 2014 · Geomatics Profession Act · IFC Performance Standard 5

Why it matters now

Servitudes are being bought, built and built on

South Africa is adding thousands of kilometres of new lines while existing servitudes fill up. The cheapest time to deal with a structure in a servitude is before the second one goes up next to it.

NTCSA, TDP 2024

A national build-out of transmission lines

The Transmission Development Plan for 2025 to 2034 plans about 14,494 km of new lines and 210 transformers, and names delays in servitude acquisition among its risks (TDP 2024).

ITP Phase 1

Independent transmission, by tender

Seven bidders were prequalified on 15 December 2025 for the first Independent Transmission Projects, with the final request for proposals expected in the 2026/27 financial year (DBSA). Every one of them needs route and servitude baselines.

Bulk water

Encroachment on the risk register

A paper by a Rand Water author at the FIG Congress 2026 reports servitude encroachment as the second risk on that utility’s strategic risk register, and a gap in encroachment data from 2017 to 2025 (FIG 2026).

Eskom

Building under lines, despite the warnings

Eskom has publicly urged people not to build structures under high-voltage power lines (Engineering News, 19 February 2024). The structures still appear between inspections.

Once a structure is occupied, resolving an unlawful occupation runs through the courts under the PIE Act, with long timelines, which is why the FIG paper argues for finding encroachment early. Knowing early gives a servitude holder more options: a conversation with the owner, a wayleave, a municipal referral, a fence, or a line diversion planned on facts.

What you receive

A dated register your servitude, wayleave and GIS teams can use

  • Each structure listed with an ID, its distance to the line, its band, its chainage and its coordinates, in WGS84 and UTM.
  • Every 500 m rated high, medium or low for encroachment density, so your servitude officers know which stretches to visit first. It is a count rule, not a safety rating.
  • New and removed structures between dated surveys, flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views.
  • The imagery named, and dated where the source gives a date.
  • A PDF report with maps, the segment table, a photo of each structure and the coordinate register, plus GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers and an interactive map file that opens in a browser.

See the full sample · How the rating works

Works with the drones you already fly

Your orthophotos, our counting and change detection

SACAA’s list of UAS operators includes utilities, mining houses, metros and engineering consultancies (SACAA). If your team already flies its own servitudes, the bottleneck is rarely the flying: it is turning a growing archive of orthophotos into a list of what is new, where, and how close it is to the line.

Send the orthophotos or GeoTIFFs you already hold. We run the structure, change and corridor analysis on them, have a person review every result and return the register and GIS layers. Between your flights, dated satellite scenes, where they exist for the stretch, show what has changed since the last one.

Analysis of your own imagery

  • Drone orthophotos and satellite GeoTIFFs you already hold
  • The same register, rating and change layers as our own surveys
  • Satellite scenes between your flights
  • Results depend on your imagery’s resolution and quality; we check a sample before we commit

Our standard

Land and assets, never people

AfriScan maps what is on the land: structures, cleared ground, excavations and tracks. We do not identify, count or follow people, and whether a structure is lawful is for you, the courts and the authorities to decide. Our registers support your wayleave, engagement, legal and community processes; they do not replace any of them.

A person reviews every result

Building datasets and detection models propose; a reviewer confirms, corrects and adds. What imagery cannot settle is listed for a ground check.

Dated and credited

Every report names its imagery and, where the source provides it, the capture date. Map-service basemaps are never passed off as survey imagery.

Scheduled, never “real‑time”

Satellites and drones capture images on particular dates, so re-surveys follow a schedule agreed with you, with a notice after each one.

POPIA-aware by design

Structures, not people; no names in the register; results only to the contacts you name; security measures at installations left out.

Satellite first, drones under Part 101

Two routes to the picture, and the rules for each

Satellite and your own imagery. A survey starts from your route file and dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or the orthophotos you already hold. No aircraft flies and nobody needs a landowner letter, however long the servitude.

Drone detail. Where a stretch needs more detail than satellite imagery shows, a drone survey captures it, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires. In South Africa that means an operator with a current UASOC and Operations Specifications from SACAA, an Air Service Licence with its South African ownership and control test, approved and registered aircraft, pilots with Remote Pilot Certificates, and the landowner’s signed permission for every flight. Flights within 50 m of people, structures or public roads need specific approvals, which matters on any servitude lined with homes.

Afridrone is working towards the operator approvals South Africa requires. Every drone proposal names the company that will fly and its approvals, so your team can check them.

The South African drone-law guide

The four approvals, what changed on 21 August 2026, the 50 m rules, key points and a 12-point checklist for anyone commissioning a drone survey, with sources, as of 26 September 2026.

For procurement and compliance teams

Supplier registration, preference points and data

Organs of state and state-owned companies buy through the Central Supplier Database and the preferential procurement rules, with B-BBEE status feeding the “specific goals” in each tender. Our procurement notes set out what applies to this kind of service, where the main buyers advertise, and what to ask any supplier for.

Notes for procurement teams

We respond to RFQs and tenders. Send your supplier or prequalification forms with your request; the proposal states which registrations are in place for your contract and which are being arranged. Include any POPIA operator terms your organisation uses.

Frequently asked questions

Which widths do you measure?

The ones in your servitudes. South African servitude widths are set in each servitude agreement and diagram, and many owners also have an internal standard or a building line. Send the widths with the route, or the servitude polygons themselves, and we report each structure’s distance to the line and the band it falls in, with up to six widths in one survey.

Does a satellite survey need SACAA approval or landowner permission?

No aircraft is flown, so the drone rules in Part 101 of the Civil Aviation Regulations, including the landowner permission SACAA requires for every flight, do not apply to the satellite work itself. Drone stretches, where you want them, are planned separately and are subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires.

We already fly our own drones. Can you work with that imagery?

Yes. Many utilities, mining houses and metros in South Africa fly their own drones. Send the orthophotos or GeoTIFFs you already have and we run the same structure, change and corridor analysis on them, with a person reviewing every result. Results depend on the imagery’s resolution and quality, which we check before we commit.

Can you tell us which structures are illegal?

No. We map what stands where, and when it first appears in the imagery. Whether a structure is lawful, authorised by a wayleave, or predates the servitude is for your property and legal teams and the authorities to decide. The register gives them a dated, located list to work from.

How does POPIA affect this work?

Imagery that shows identifiable people, homes or businesses can contain personal information, so the survey should run under a written operator agreement (POPIA s21), and results go only to the contacts you name. Our registers describe structures, not people, and carry no names. If you plan to use a register as evidence about unlawful conduct, POPIA’s prior-authorisation rule may apply to your organisation, so take advice first. See POPIA and aerial imagery.

Is the register a survey we can register against the title deed?

No. Surveys for registrable diagrams and the fixing of servitude boundaries are reserved to professional land surveyors, with Surveyor-General approval of the diagram. Our registers are monitoring and planning records built from imagery. They show your surveyor and your wayleave officers where to look, and they support your legal and community processes.

Know what stands in your servitude while it is still one structure, not a settlement.

Send the line or pipeline route (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage), the province and the servitude widths that apply. Tell us if you already fly drones. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
